clarifyingQuestions: How is the black-box function passed in a test (a callable, or a description of F)?
Must the answer be a specific point, or is any point within eps accepted?
Which point is returned when F is flat over several grid points?
hints: A convex function restricted to evenly spaced points is still convex: it decreases, then stays flat, then increases.
Compare F at two neighbouring grid points: the sign tells you which side of the minimum you are on.
Binary search for the first index j with F(x_j) <= F(x_{j+1}); if none exists the last grid point is the answer.
Evaluate F as the maximum of slope * x + intercept over all lines; keep everything in exact integers.
invariants: every index left of the answer has F(x_j) > F(x_{j+1})
every index from the answer on has F(x_j) <= F(x_{j+1})
chooseWhen: The function is unimodal (convex) and each evaluation is expensive
tradeoffs: Binary search on neighbour differences needs two evaluations per step but no derivative
hack2hire:68e9a2a2149617c9114ece06.variantLabel: Inferred: max-of-lines function, leftmost grid minimiser

clarifyingQuestions: What is returned when the call cannot be kept alive?
Is a battery that becomes ready exactly when it is needed usable?
Are all batteries charged at the start?
hints: Simulate the first full pass: every battery is charged, so only the running total matters.
From the second pass on, battery i waits exactly (total usage - usage[i]) minutes between being drained and being needed again.
If any battery cannot recharge in that window, the call can only reach as far as the first such battery in pass two.
Otherwise passes repeat: count whole passes arithmetically and finish with a binary search on the prefix sums.
invariants: powered time after j insertions equals the prefix sum of usage along the circular order
the idle window of battery i is the same in every pass after the first
chooseWhen: A periodic process can be characterised by one period plus a warm-up
tradeoffs: The closed form avoids a simulation whose length grows with duration, at the cost of a careful case split
hack2hire:69a4da066e73e4abccc9c43f.variantLabel: Inferred: count insertions in circular order with recharge feasibility

constraints: tree depth at most 90 levels (JSON nesting stays below 200)
clarifyingQuestions: Is the distance counted in edges or in nodes?
Are both values guaranteed to be present?
Can p equal q?
hints: The path between two nodes goes up to their lowest common ancestor and down again.
distance(p, q) = depth(p) + depth(q) - 2 * depth(lca).
Record each node's parent and depth with an explicit stack, then lift the deeper node until both depths match.
Walk both nodes up together until they meet; that meeting node is the LCA.
invariants: after lifting, both pointers have equal depth
the walk ends at the lowest common ancestor
chooseWhen: A single distance query on a rooted tree
tradeoffs: Parent pointers cost O(n) memory but make every later query cheap
hack2hire:696eb8a4920c39311a3992be.variantLabel: Inferred level 1: distance between two nodes

clarifyingQuestions: Do the groups possibly overlap?

clarifyingQuestions: Is the price continuous or integer-valued?
How should the expected value be printed (decimals, rounding)?
May k exceed n?
hints: Let E[i][j] be the optimal expected cost of i remaining units with j fixed-price uses left.
Seeing price x, pay x and go to E[i-1][j], or pay p and go to E[i-1][j-1]; take the cheaper.
min(x + A, B) switches from the first to the second branch at one threshold price, so the sum over prices splits into an arithmetic series and a constant block.
Keep numerators over the common denominator m**i so every step stays in exact integers; round only at the end.
invariants: E[i][j] is non-increasing in j
every stored numerator is an exact integer over m**i
chooseWhen: Optimal stopping / option problems with a small state
tradeoffs: Exact rationals avoid floating-point drift but need big integers

constraints: entry = [id, price, items]; ids unique [A-Za-z0-9_]{1,12}; price 1..10**6 (integer cents)
items: 1 to 10 unique names [a-z]{1,10} joined by commas
clarifyingQuestions: May an order include items the customer did not ask for?
Can the same entry be bought twice?
What is returned if some item is unavailable?
hints: With at most 12 wanted items, a set of covered items fits in a bitmask.
Reduce each entry to the mask of wanted items it contains and drop entries with an empty mask.
dp[mask] = cheapest cost to cover at least mask; relax dp[mask | e] from dp[mask] in increasing mask order.
Keep only the cheapest entry per distinct mask to shrink the inner loop.
invariants: dp[mask] only decreases
mask | e >= mask, so increasing order processes every state after all its predecessors
chooseWhen: Set cover with a small universe
tradeoffs: Exponential in the number of wanted items but linear in menu size

constraints: entry = [id, price, items]; ids unique [A-Za-z0-9_]{1,12}; price 1..10**6 (integer cents)
items: 1 to 10 unique names [a-z]{1,10} joined by commas
clarifyingQuestions: Which secondary objective breaks price ties?
Is the count of entries or of items reported?

hints: The DP state is the same as for level 1.
Store a pair (price, count) per mask and compare pairs lexicographically.

constraints: entry = [id, price, items]; ids unique; price 1..10**6
at most 5000 optimal combinations in the generated cases
clarifyingQuestions: Must each wanted item be covered exactly once, or at least once?
Are only the cheapest combinations wanted, or all of them?
How are the combinations ordered?
hints: Every exact cover contains exactly one entry with the lowest uncovered item.
Branch only on entries containing that item and disjoint from what is covered: no combination is produced twice.
Memoise best[mask], the cheapest exact cover of the remaining items.
Enumerate again, following only entries e with price(e) + best[rest] == best[mask]; sort ids inside each set and then the sets.
invariants: each produced set covers each wanted item exactly once
the lowest-item rule makes every set appear once
chooseWhen: Enumerating all optimal solutions of a small exact-cover problem
tradeoffs: Two passes (value, then enumeration) avoid storing every partial combination

constraints: balls contains only R and W
clarifyingQuestions: Is there a cap on the answer?
Is an empty string possible?
Must the block be at a fixed place?
hints: Red balls never need to pass each other, so the i-th red ball ends at start + i.
Subtract i from the i-th red position; the problem becomes moving points to one common value.
The sum of absolute deviations is minimised at the median.
Sum |shifted_i - median|; the result fits in 2**53.
invariants: shifted positions are non-decreasing
the median minimises the sum of absolute deviations

tradeoffs: The median trick is O(n) but only works because relative order is preserved

constraints: hierarchy depth up to 100000 (rows, not nested JSON)
clarifyingQuestions: Is "can defeat" transitive down the hierarchy?
What is returned when there are no hostile monsters?
In which order are the names returned?
hints: A monster can defeat everything below it, so it must be an ancestor of every hostile monster.
Count hostile monsters in each subtree with a post-order traversal.
A non-hostile node qualifies when the hostile count strictly below it equals the total count.
Use an explicit stack: the hierarchy can be a long chain.
invariants: below[u] = sum over children of (below[c] + hostile(c))
the qualifying nodes form a prefix of a root path
chooseWhen: Subtree aggregates on a tree
tradeoffs: One pass with counts beats per-node searches but needs a child-to-parent order
hack2hire:6779c17edcf91f8e3c1c310f.variantLabel: Inferred level 1: monsters that defeat every hostile

clarifyingQuestions: Does every monster have a cost?
Can one chosen monster defeat many hostiles?
What if a hostile monster cannot be reached by any non-hostile ancestor?
hints: Choosing u defeats everything below it, so inside its subtree nothing else is needed.
Otherwise every child subtree must be handled on its own, and a hostile child itself can then never be covered.
need[u] = min(cost(u), sum of children contributions); a hostile child contributes infinity.
The answer is need[root]; a hostile root is never covered.
invariants: need[u] = 0 when no hostile lies strictly below u
need[u] is finite whenever u is non-hostile and below[u] > 0
chooseWhen: Tree covering with costs
tradeoffs: Bottom-up DP is linear but needs an infinity sentinel for impossible subtrees

clarifyingQuestions: Do overlapping occurrences count?
What if n is larger than the string?
Is the comparison by code point?
hints: There are len(str) - n + 1 windows of length n.
Count each window in a hash map.
Keep the best window: higher count wins, and on equal counts the smaller string wins.
Return "" when there is no window.
invariants: the map holds the count of every window seen so far
chooseWhen: Counting fixed-length windows
tradeoffs: Slicing costs O(n) per window; a rolling hash would be faster for long windows but needs collision handling

clarifyingQuestions: How are segment sizes distributed when n is not divisible by k?
Is the merge also parallel?
May k exceed n?
hints: Segment i gets floor(n / k) elements, plus one for the first n mod k segments.
Sort each segment on its own copy: no segment reads another.
Merge sorted runs two at a time; each round halves the number of runs.
The merge is the only step that sees elements from different segments.
invariants: after each merge round every run is sorted
the multiset of elements never changes
chooseWhen: Parallel sort with a final merge
tradeoffs: Pairwise merge rounds cost O(n log k) after the segment sorts

clarifyingQuestions: What is output when processing an offset does not allow a commit?

hints: Keep the set of completed offsets.

clarifyingQuestions: Is arr a string or a list of characters?
Does the count include the query node itself?
Can the tree be a long chain?
hints: A multiset of letters can form a palindrome iff at most one letter has an odd count.
Store letter parities as a 26-bit mask; the mask of a path segment is an xor of two root prefixes.
During a DFS keep a count of the prefix masks of the current root path; for v on that path, segment q..v has mask P[q] xor P[parent(v)].
Count prefixes equal to P[q] or differing in one bit; use an explicit stack because the tree may be a chain.
invariants: the counter holds exactly the masks P[parent(v)] for v on the current root path
a mask with at most one set bit means palindrome-able
chooseWhen: Path queries about letter parities
tradeoffs: 27 hash lookups per node trade memory for a linear-time pass

clarifyingQuestions: When does the reduction stop: one digit or two?
Is the sum taken mod 10?
Are leading zeros kept?
hints: One round maps a string of length L to length L - 1, so L - 2 rounds are needed.
Digit 0 of the result is sum over i of C(L - 2, i) * d[i] mod 10, a row of Pascal's triangle.
Compute C mod 2 and C mod 5 with Lucas' theorem and combine them by the Chinese remainder theorem.
Digit 1 uses the same coefficients on d[i + 1].
invariants: the rounds are linear with Pascal-triangle coefficients
Lucas gives C mod prime from base-p digits
chooseWhen: Repeated linear reductions over many rounds
tradeoffs: The binomial form is far faster than O(L**2) rounds but needs number theory
